title: 梁書 54 — Qin Lun 秦論, a merchant of Da Qin at the court of Sun Quan, 226 CE, and the trade route that brought him
language_note: Literary Chinese, compiled 635 CE by Yao Silian, recording an event of 226 CE. The excerpt is taken from the Wenyuange Siku Quanshu recension via Kanripo, whose orthography is visible in it — 黄 for 黃, 来 for 來, 吴 for 吳, 㑹 for 會, 絶 for 絕, 謡 for 謠.
date: Compiled 635 CE (Liang shu, juan 54, 諸夷傳); the episode it records is dated in the text to the fifth year of Huangwu, 226 CE.
original_text_excerpt: 其國人行賈往往至扶南日南交趾其南徼諸國人少有到大秦者孫權黄武五年有大秦賈人字秦論来到交趾交趾太守吴邈遣送詣權權問方土謡俗論具以事對時諸葛恪討丹陽獲黝歙短人論見之曰大秦希見此人權以男女各十人差吏㑹稽劉咸送論咸於道物故論乃徑還本國
original_text_note:
Verbatim Literary Chinese, 113 characters, COPIED BY HAND from Kanripo raw.githubusercontent.com/kanripo/KR2a0018/master/KR2a0018_054.txt on 2026-09-01, spanning the page boundary marked <pb:KR2a0018_WYG_054-21b>.

EDITORIAL ACTS, DECLARED. Kanripo's ¶ line markers and its <pb:...> page marker are removed and the words they split are closed up. No punctuation is added: the source carries none, and the sentence divisions a reader sees in the translation are the translator's, not the text's.

THE RECENSION IS THE WENYUANGE SIKU QUANSHU AND THAT IS A STATED, UNCOLLATED BOUNDARY. The page marker names it — WYG — and F4_CANDIDATES records the reason it matters: the Qianlong editors are known to have altered passages about foreign peoples, and this is a passage about foreign peoples. No collation against a Zhonghua Shuju edition was performed, because none is openly reachable from this project. The reading published here is Kanripo's, the boundary is named, and correcting it is a matter of somebody opening a book this session could not.
reference_translation:
[6] The merchants of this country frequently visit Fu-nan [Siam, Cambodja?] Jih-nan [Annam] and Chiao-chih [Tung-king]; [7] but few of the inhabitants of these southern frontier states have come to Ta-ts'in. [8] During the 5th year of the Huang-wu period of the reign of Sun-ch'üan [=A.D. 226] a merchant of Ta-ts'in, whose name was Ts'in-lun, came to Chiao-chih [Tung-king]; the prefect [t'ai-shou] of Chiao-chih, Wu Miao, sent him to Sun-ch'üan [the Wu emperor], who asked him for a report on his native country and its people. [9] Ts'in-lun prepared a statement, and replied. [10] At the time Chu-ko K'o chastised Tan-yang and they had caught blackish coloured dwarfs. When Ts'in-lun saw them he said that in Ta-ts'in these men are rarely seen. Sun-ch'üan then sent male and female dwarfs, ten of each, in charge of an officer, Liu Hsien of Hui-chi [a district in Chêkiang], to accompany Ts'in-lun. Liu Hsien died on the road, whereupon Ts'in-lun returned direct to his native country.

HIRTH DOES NOT SETTLE WHERE FU-NAN WAS, AND HIS BRACKETS SAY SO. Against 扶南 he prints two alternatives and a question mark — 'Fu-nan [Siam, Cambodja?]' — offering Siam and Cambodja and choosing neither. The Chinese characters are not in doubt; what is uncertain is which modern country they answer to, and the translator marked that uncertainty rather than resolving it. THIS IS THE WEAKEST GLOSS IN THIS CORPUS and the record says so itself: every other gloss-capable record here carries a dispute about how to READ its source text, and this one carries a translator's hedge about a geographical identification. It is declared, and it is declared with the discount attached.

AND ONE RENDERING IN THIS PASSAGE IS OLDER THAN IT LOOKS. 獲黝歙短人 is given above as 'they had caught blackish coloured dwarfs', reading 黝 as a colour. 黝 and 歙 are also the names of two counties of Danyang commandery, on which reading the sentence means the short people of Yi and She — local people of the Wu heartland, not dark-skinned ones. This record does NOT adjudicate between them, because no published alternative reachable from this project states the second, and a translation this corpus supplied itself would be worth nothing. See FINDING 55.
translation_source:
Friedrich Hirth, China and the Roman Orient: Researches into their Ancient and Mediaeval Relations as Represented in Old Chinese Records (Shanghai and Hong Kong, 1885), section H, pp. 47-48, translating Liang-shu ch. 54, lieh-chuan 48. Read from the PAGE IMAGES on archive.org (item chinaandromanor01hirtgoog), NOT from that item's _djvu.txt, per FINDING 53. F4_CANDIDATES gives this as p. 46; the passage is on pp. 47-48 and that is corrected here.

IT IS THE ONLY REACHABLE ENGLISH. Four searches found no second open translation of this passage. Leslie & Gardiner, The Roman Empire in Chinese Sources (Rome, 1996), is the standard translation-corpus of exactly this material and is print-only; nothing available to this project can establish what it says. That boundary is stated for the same reason ruling 57 makes the verbatim_machine_english tier state its own.
reference_translation_note:
CAPTURED BY THE CURATOR FROM THE PAGE IMAGES AND THEN DIFFED AGAINST THEM, which is FINDING 50's arrangement and its third measurement. The typing diverged from the page in six places across one paragraph: 'Ts'in-lin' and 'Ts'in-lub' for Ts'in-lun, 'chastied' for chastised, 'colored' for coloured, a dropped 'that' in 'he said that in Ta-ts'in', and a dropped 'direct' in 'returned direct to his native country'. Every one was put back to the curator and confirmed by the curator.

Two of the six were not cosmetic. The merchant's NAME was wrong twice in two different ways, and it is the name this record exists for and the token a retriever keys on. And 'direct' is a claim about the route: Hirth's Ts'in-lun goes straight home after his escort dies, and without the word the sentence merely says he went home. 'coloured' becoming 'colored' is the same class as the circumflex dropped from Tâ Ts'in on record 33 — a silent modernisation of the source's orthography by the human path, where record 33's was by the machine path.

Hirth's footnotes 1 and 2 on p. 48 identify Chu-ko K'o as the nephew of Chu-ko Liang and gloss Tan-yang as Kiang-nan. They are his apparatus rather than his rendering and are not reproduced in this field; they are named here so a reader knows what was left out and why.

notes:
F4 Part 2, record 34, and the record that takes East Asia to FOUR source-language records — the per-region floor, met.

WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT ROME, AND WHY THE EXCERPT STARTS WHERE IT DOES. This is the most concrete Roman person in the East Asian record: a merchant of Da Qin who reaches Jiaozhi in 226, is forwarded to Sun Quan, is questioned about the customs of his own country, is shown captured short-statured people and remarks that Da Qin rarely sees such people, and is sent home with an escort who dies on the road. The excerpt deliberately opens two clauses earlier, at 其國人行賈往往至扶南日南交趾, because those clauses say the traffic was ROUTINE — merchants of that country regularly reach Funan, Rinan and Jiaozhi — and few southerners go the other way. Without them Qin Lun reads as a curiosity; with them he is one instance of a pattern the compiler thought worth stating, which is what this corpus is actually about.

GLOSS-CAPABLE, DECLARED, AND DECLARED AS THE WEAKEST ONE HERE. Ruling 62 governs how it is read and F4_RESULT carries the discount rather than reporting three equivalent cases. The hedge is Hirth's 'Fu-nan [Siam, Cambodja?]' — two published alternatives and a question mark, inside the chunked reference_translation. What it is not is a dispute about how to read the Chinese: 扶南 is not in doubt. Every other gloss record in this corpus carries a contested READING, and this one carries a translator's uncertainty about a modern identification.

THE THING THAT WOULD HAVE MADE A BETTER GLOSS AND COULD NOT BE USED. Hirth renders 獲黝歙短人 as 'blackish coloured dwarfs'; the same characters are the names of two Danyang counties. That is a genuine alternative construal with a real difference in meaning, and no published statement of it is reachable from this project, so supplying it would have been this corpus writing its own scholarship into a chunked field. FINDING 55 is what that cost.

RULING 55, again. This is the second Literary Chinese record about Rome entering the index in this tranche, and its query is written to be about the same subject as both china-describes-rome pairs. The prediction is unread until the ranking check runs at the close.

subject_places.name: Da Qin (大秦)
subject_places.note: 大秦, the country the merchant comes FROM and the country whose merchants the passage says regularly reach the southern ports. It is what the other two places are directional relative to, and ingest.verify is why this entry exists: two places carried destination and waypoint roles with no focus, which names one end of an edge and no other. TREATED AS eastasia-01-weilue ALREADY TREATS IT — ground `regional`, no gazetteer id, because it is a polity rather than a settlement. That is NOT in tension with record 33, where 大秦國 was left out: what was declined there was a gazetteer ID, which would have silently settled that record's gloss in a field carrying no apparatus. A regional ground with no id settles nothing, and was available there too. Record 33's note says 'deliberately not placed' where it should have said 'deliberately not RESOLVED', and that wording is corrected in this same commit.

subject_places.name: Jiaozhi (交趾)
subject_places.note: 交趾, where the merchant lands and where the prefect Wu Miao forwards him onward. Stated in the text twice. GROUND IS `regional` BECAUSE NO GAZETTEER ID WAS SOUGHT, and that is the honest wording rather than the one the first draft used. That draft declared ground `stated` with no id and an argument about not placing the journey's middle without its ends; ingest.verify refused it, correctly -- `stated` names a specific place and so requires an id, and if none can be found the honest ground is `regional`. The check's own sentence is the reason this field now reads as it does. Declining to LOOK and failing to FIND are different things, and only the second is what `regional` is for, so this note says which one happened.

subject_places.name: Funan (扶南)
subject_places.note: DELIBERATELY NOT RESOLVED, and that is this record's gloss rather than an omission. Hirth prints 'Fu-nan [Siam, Cambodja?]' — two alternatives and a question mark. A gazetteer id here would settle, in a field no reader argues with and that carries no apparatus, precisely the question the reference_translation holds open. The same decision was taken for 大秦國 on record 33.
